betterCitation: Elizabeth Cary, The Tragedy of Mariam, the Chorus closing Act 4, lines 1 to 4 (Chorus) (1613 quarto)
reason:
The attribution survives, and it survives the one trap that matters here, which the verifier's note never mentions. These four lines circulated for a century in anthologies as ‘Revenge of Injuries’ by ‘Elizabeth, Lady Carew’, and that ghost is still live on the open web: my own search for the line came back insisting the poem belongs to a sixteenth-century Lady Carew, wife of Sir Nicholas Carew, and not to Elizabeth Cary at all. The verifier got this right. The lines are the Chorus that closes Act 4 of The Tragedy of Mariam, and I confirmed it in the quarto itself.

WHAT I READ. First, the Malone Society Reprint scan the verifier cited, archive.org tragedyofmariam100caryrich, downloaded and read this run. The Chorus stands where claimed, immediately after Mariam's exit at the close of Act 4. Second, and this is the witness the verifier did not have, the transcription of the 1613 quarto at A Celebration of Women Writers, digital.library.upenn.edu/women/cary/mariam/mariam.html, whose title page reads ‘London: Printed by Thomas Creede for Richard Hawkins, 1613’. Two independent transcriptions of the same quarto.

THE LOCATOR AND THE COLON HOLD. The correction the verifier made is right: line 2 ends in a colon. Both witnesses agree. The Malone OCR reads ‘Is fcorniug to reuenge an iniurie:’ and the UPenn transcription reads ‘Is scorning to revenge an injurie:’. Good catch, and the stanza is a sestet rhyming ababcc, so cutting after line 4 is a clean sense unit, with ‘And tis a firmer conquest truely sed, / To winne the heart, then ouerthrow the head.’ left off.

WHY I REFUTE, GROUND ONE: THE QUOTATION DROPS PUNCTUATION THE QUARTO HAS. Both witnesses print a mark at the end of line 1. UPenn gives ‘The fairest action of our humane life,’ with a comma; the Malone OCR gives a full point there, which is the routine OCR misread of a comma. The card prints ‘our human life’ bare, with nothing after it. That comma is not incidental: it is the one that separates the subject from ‘Is scorning’ in the quarto's pointing, and it is the reason the colon in line 2 is a colon and not a semicolon. Take the comma away and keep the colon and the line is punctuated as no edition punctuates it.

GROUND TWO: THE NOTE MAKES A CONFIDENT CLAIM THAT IS FALSE. The note says line 2 ends in a colon ‘in the 1613 quarto and in modern editions alike’. The modern circulating text does not. The standard modernised text, the one the anthologies carry under the title ‘Revenge of Injuries’ and the one reproduced across the web, reads ‘Is scorning to revenge an injury;’ with a semicolon, and reads ‘The fairest action of our human life’ with no comma. That is where the card's line 1 comes from. So the shipped text is a hybrid: modern-anthology pointing in line 1, quarto pointing in line 2, and the note asserts an agreement between the two that does not exist. Under this track's own standard that is the failure being guarded against, a confident statement about a source that the source does not support.

GROUND THREE, SMALLER: THE MALONE LINE NUMBER IS OFF, AND THE ACT NUMBERING IS A GUESS. The evidence says ‘beside line 1905’. Counting the reprint's marginal numerals, 1900 stands beside ‘This curse of thine shall be return'd on thee:’, and 1910 beside ‘If we a worthy enemie doe finde’, which is the seventh line of the Chorus. That fixes the speech heading at 1903 and the four quoted lines at 1904 to 1907, not 1905. The evidence's own ‘numbered about 628 to 631 in act line numbering’ says ‘about’, which is an admission that it was not counted. Neither number reaches the card, so this alone would not sink it, but it shows the locator was estimated rather than read.

GROUND FOUR, FORMAT: THE SPEAKER IS IN THE WRONG PLACE. Rule 5 puts the speaker in parentheses after the locator. The card reads ‘... lines 1 to 4 (1613) (Chorus)’, which puts a bare date between the locator and the speaker. The file's own settled practice is speaker first and the imprint or translation last: ‘... after the first shark (Santiago) (Scribner, 1952)’, ‘... Adventure Number Two (Commander Caractacus Pott) (Jonathan Cape, 1964)’, ‘... Book II, Prose IV (Philosophy) (trans. H. R. James, 1897)’. This one is inverted. It also says ‘the chorus that closes the act’ and then ‘(Chorus)’, which is the same fact twice inside 106 characters.

WHAT PASSES, FOR THE RECORD. shipped.js: shipped [], near [], elizabeth cary at 0 of 3, not banned, so she is free and she is a woman, which the month's floor wants. Scope is clean: drama, 1613, not scripture, not film, not lyric, not proverb, not business, not oratory. Publishable: there is nothing in these four lines that needs a warning, and the note's gloss on the Chorus as a company who judge by their own lights is fair and is the right kind of caution. The tag Drama is the form of the work. The source line leads with the name, carries no em dash, uses curly quotes, and is 106 characters. Theme fit is real if slightly sideways: the stanza's argument is that forgiving is the braver conquest, which is Courage in Trial read as the courage not to strike back, and the sestet's later ‘Who would a worthy courage overthrow’ confirms the Chorus is talking about courage.

HOW TO FIX IT, NOT KILL IT. Restore the quarto comma and keep the quarto colon, so that the pointing comes from one witness rather than two: ‘The fairest action of our human life, / Is scorning to revenge an injury: / For who forgives without a further strife, / His adversary’s heart to him doth tie.’ Lines 3 and 4 already match the quarto exactly, comma and full point. Then fix the source line to the one in betterCitation, which puts the speaker after the locator and names the quarto as the text, and rewrite the note to say plainly that the spelling is modernised from the 1613 quarto (humane, injurie, adversaries), that the pointing is the quarto's, and that the modernised anthology text, which travels under the title ‘Revenge of Injuries’ and often under the wrong name ‘Elizabeth, Lady Carew’, prints a semicolon in line 2 and no comma in line 1. That last sentence is worth a line of the note on its own: it is the trap a reader will hit if they go looking.
